newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo dinar black market rate picks up to 3.5/DM.
newsitem.headline: Yugo dinar black market rate picks up to 3.5/DM.

text.p: Yugoslavia's dinar black market rate strengthened to 3.5-3.6 to the German mark on lack of cash in circulation, dealers said on Friday.
Earlier this week, the dinar was changing hands at 3.6-3.7 to the mark.
"There is almost no cash around. There is an occasional buyer, but it's hundreds, not thousands of marks they buy," a dealer told Reuters.
Dealers expected a slight downward correction in the dinar rate after the government paid out pensions earlier this week.

"Whenever there is a big dinar pay-out -- pensions, credits, investments -- we look for more cash on the streets, but it seems they really do not let any more cash than they say they paid," the dealer said.

Yugoslavia's currency resumed its upward trend after sinking to as low as 4.3 to the German mark in the early days of 1997 when several hundred million dinars flooded the black market during eight days of New Year and Christmas holidays.

In January, the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) took measures to stabilise the dinar and restore financial discipline by halting further increases in the M1 money supply, preventing imbalances on the banks' giro-accounts and halting insolvent banks from further lending activity.
The NBY reduced the M1 money supply to 5.157 billion dinars ($906 million) at the end of February from 5.495 billion at the end of December.
Yugoslavia's new finance minister Bozidar Gazivoda said M1 money supply has been kept stable since the beginning of 1997.

"There is no particular answer why the dinar strengthened on the black market in recent days. There must be some interruption in money flows, but the NBY has not changed anything," Gazivoda, who is also an outgoing NBY deputy governor, told Reuters.
In its 1997 economic policy, the Yugoslav government has vowed to keep the dinar stable and fixed at 3.3 to the mark.

The dinar was last devalued by 70 percent in November 1995 to bring it in line with the then black market rate. Its street value remained stable at 3.4-3.5 until last November after devaluation fears mounted ahead of general elections.

"We keep the dinar stable with relatively simple instruments, that is by controlling the money supply. There is no developed financial market. We try to do something with securities, but could do a lot more," he told Reuters.
Gazivoda insisted that keeping the dinar rate fixed was the only way to keep it stable while the country was denied access to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and world markets.

"We keep it fixed because we know it is a preparation for a final decision when we rejoin the IMF whose key demand is to have the currency rate established by the market," he said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
